_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-05 15:23:05Z)**_

Yes. Using Böckeler’s article as the benchmark, DeadReckon already implements its central feedforward-and-feedback model quite directly—not merely by analogy.

The strongest alignment is that the same frozen acceptance contract operates in both directions:

```text
goal + acceptance contract + skill
                ↓ feedforward
             coding agent
                ↓
      dr-gate deterministic checks
                ↓ feedback on failure
      fresh semantic completion judge
                ↓ feedback on “revise”
         signed receipt + promotion
```

The article defines guides as controls applied before action and sensors as observations used for self-correction afterward. [Harness engineering: Feedforward and Feedback](https://martinfowler.com/articles/harness-engineering.html#FeedforwardAndFeedback)

| Article concept | In DeadReckon | How |
|---|---|---|
| Outer user harness | Fully baked in | DeadReckon wraps existing coding-agent CLIs and owns their execution boundary, verification and promotion. |
| Feedforward guides | Fully baked in | Every worker prompt receives the goal, acceptance criteria, selected skill and previous feedback. See [turn_loop.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:2795) and [default-coding/SKILL.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/skills/default-coding/SKILL.md:15). |
| Guide/sensor coherence | Particularly strong | Before execution, DeadReckon freezes the goal, contract, policy and source identity and binds them by digest. The exact contract shown to the worker is later evaluated by the gate. See [job.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/job.rs:223). |
| Computational feedback sensor | Fully baked in | `dr-gate` deterministically executes the approved checks, validates tamper evidence and only then signs the result. See [gate.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/gate.rs:653). Default test contracts are detected across Rust, Node, Go, Python, JVM and other ecosystems in [acceptance_defaults.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/acceptance_defaults.rs:80). |
| Inferential feedback sensor | Fully baked in | A fresh, read-only model receives the goal, contract, diff, deterministic marker, authority and implementation notes. It must return `achieved`, `revise` or `uncertain`. See [semantic_judge.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/semantic_judge.rs:189) and its judge prompt at [semantic_judge.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/semantic_judge.rs:865). |
| Closed self-correction loop | Fully baked in for Single Jobs | A gate failure is appended to the history and execution continues with another worker turn. See [turn_loop.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:5777). A semantic `revise` similarly feeds its summary and missing requirements into the next turn at [turn_loop.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:5276). |
| Fail-closed human boundary | Fully baked in | An uncertain or unavailable judge becomes `NEEDS_REVIEW`; it cannot silently promote. The human still defines/approves “done” and chooses whether to apply the verified result. |
| Steering the harness from repeated failures | Present but experimental | `learn index` extracts repeated failures, acceptance gaps, slow paths and other signals; `learn propose` turns them into cited proposals; `improve self` evaluates an isolated candidate. See [AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md:2549). The project itself currently labels this capability experimental and potentially removable in [MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md:198). |
| “Keep quality left” | Partial | The contract exists before the first turn and checks run before promotion, but sensors generally run at a completion boundary—not continuously after each edit or tool call. |
| Maintainability, architecture and behaviour harnesses | Infrastructure exists; policy is mostly user-supplied | DeadReckon provides tests, file/content checks, builds and arbitrary shell checks. It does not inherently know a project’s architectural boundaries, performance requirements, mutation-testing policy or product behaviour unless those are encoded in its acceptance contract. |
| Continuous drift/runtime sensing | Not currently inherent | DeadReckon monitors its own job lifecycle, processes, spend and containment, but it does not continuously monitor deployed SLOs, dependency drift, dead code or production behaviour and automatically start corrective work. |
| Harness templates | Partial | Detected default contracts, acceptance packs and reusable skills resemble pieces of a template, but there is no first-class bundled “service topology + guides + sensors” abstraction of the kind the article describes. |

Two important qualifications:

- The full two-key loop belongs to durable, contained Jobs. Preview, in-place, `--sandbox none` and legacy compatibility paths are explicitly untrusted escape hatches.
- Graph and Campaign parents behave slightly differently: semantic `revise` starts a bounded parent-only repair, but a deterministic parent-gate failure stops rather than automatically repairing. That distinction is documented in [CONCEPTS.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/CONCEPTS.md:178).

The clearest gap against the article is the quality of computational feedback delivered back to the LLM. DeadReckon captures clipped stdout and stderr for gate checks in [gate.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/gate.rs:1264), but the retry history currently receives primarily the first failed check’s short `detail` string—not the useful compiler/test output. The article specifically recommends sensor output optimized for model consumption. Injecting a structured failure packet containing the command, exit status, relevant stdout/stderr and suggested correction would make DeadReckon’s existing loop materially stronger.

So the short verdict is: **feedforward, feedback, computational/inferential pairing, bounded self-correction and fail-closed human escalation are foundational DeadReckon architecture. Continuous sensing, first-class architecture/maintainability profiles and automated cross-run harness evolution are only partial or absent.**

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-05 19:58:48Z)**_

The audit confirms this is a systemic START orchestration problem. Fixing the expired timer alone would stop the immediate loop, but would not consolidate the recurring START failures.

## What happened in your session

Two distinct failures occurred:

1. Contract rejection  
   Draft → critic → redraft completed, but the redraft still failed deterministic coverage/linting.

   For this goal, the likely missing evidence is the macOS/Flappy/exceptional-graphics clause; your operator wording mainly covered networking. DeadReckon calculates the exact uncovered clauses and weak checks, then discards them and reports only the generic error at [acceptance.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/acceptance.rs:1197).

2. Impossible recovery  
   `start` creates one absolute 1,200-second budget at [start.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/start.rs:4112). Retry and Revise loop through [start.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/start.rs:3263) using a copy of that same expired deadline.

   Therefore both choices fail before another provider request can start. Operator thinking time also consumes the deadline, contrary to the documented policy.

The regression arose at the seam between:

- `f3a97fb`, which added Retry/Revise recovery.
- `2f26e8d`, which introduced the shared fixed admission deadline.

## START machinery and dependencies

```text
source resolution
  → course planning
  → launch-path selection
  → provider/team selection
  → contract draft → critic → redraft → deterministic floor
  → contract review
  → final confirmation
  → supervisor/helper readiness
  → source and contract freezing
  → durable Job creation
  → dispatch and supervision
```

The recent failure history falls into five coupled clusters:

| Cluster | Examples | Shared boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Provider routing and protocol | `f7dcca5`, `f5b24ef`, `d2c087e`, `a05c34f` | Selected team, authoring provider and provider schema |
| Admission clocks and recovery | `f3a97fb`, `17e64fe`, `2f26e8d` | Planner budget, authoring budget and legal recovery actions |
| Source and contract ownership | `c00e4ba`, `515b999`, `56078fa` | Inspection source, generated contract and Job bundle |
| Binary identity and liveness | `cfaf29b`, `bbffb62`, `05f0525`, `b003479` | CLI, helper and supervisor identity |
| Post-admission runtime | `bb594a3`, `69a5099` | Durable Job deadlines and process containment |

The shared cause is that guided START is not represented as one typed, durable admission transaction. Its source, team, route, contract, budget and recovery state are held or reconstructed across `start.rs`, `acceptance.rs`, `job.rs`, supervisor code and provider adapters.

## Other consolidation-level defects found

- Course planning can consume the entire 1,200-second admission budget because its nominal 300-second route cap is bypassed.
- A rejected draft’s exact lint findings and provider output are deleted.
- The suggested `def-done refine` command is invalid when the rejected fresh contract was never written.
- Failed guided starts are not resumable; source, shape and team choices exist only in memory.
- Fresh-source contract detection can inspect the current project even though the Job will receive an empty source.
- Prompt suppression has two authorities, so ostensibly non-interactive modes can still reach a provider rescue prompt.
- Contract files are written before final launch confirmation.
- Several important Job validations happen only after the user traverses the complete wizard.

## What would count as a consolidated fix

I recommend introducing one `StartAdmission` record that owns:

- An immutable resolved source.
- Course and execution-team selection.
- A distinct contract-authoring route.
- Typed phase outcomes and failure causes.
- Preserved draft, critic and deterministic findings.
- Separate overall admission, per-phase and authorized-retry limits.
- Recovery actions derived from the failure type and guaranteed to be executable.
- A resumable checkpoint.
- An atomic handoff into exactly one durable Job.

The immediate repair should be made inside that boundary:

- Stop reusing an expired absolute deadline.
- Exclude operator wait from automated-work accounting.
- Never offer Retry when no runnable budget remains.
- Treat deterministic rejection as `RevisionRequired(findings)`, not generic `CliError`.
- Carry missing clauses and weak-check indices into the revision prompt.
- Stage generated contract artifacts until approval.

## Required proof

The existing tests do not cover this. The three Flappy-named regression tests pre-write a valid contract and bypass contract authoring and recovery entirely.

The decisive test needs to reproduce your journey:

```text
empty non-git directory
→ InitGit selected
→ full-plan + Codex team
→ weak draft
→ critic
→ weak redraft near budget limit
→ actionable findings shown
→ operator revises
→ permitted new provider attempt
→ contract accepted
→ supervisor admitted
→ exactly one Graph Job ID
```

It should run with a fake clock and scripted provider, with failure injection at every START phase. TTY, plain and JSON modes should expose the same phase, cause and executable next action.

No files were changed and no tests completed during this read-only diagnosis. The relevant files are also identical on local `main`, `origin/main`, and `release-0.8.2`; there is no pending upstream fix to absorb.

explain simply what happens today versus what should happen

---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-05 20:14:00Z)**_

Today:

1. DeadReckon asks Codex to draft the definition of done.
2. Codex critiques it and tries one rewrite.
3. DeadReckon rejects the rewrite, but hides the specific reasons.
4. By then, the shared 20-minute timer has expired.
5. DeadReckon still offers Retry and Revise.
6. Both options reuse the expired timer, so they fail immediately.
7. Restarting `deadreckon start` makes you repeat the entire setup.

What should happen:

1. DeadReckon drafts and checks the definition of done.
2. If it fails, it shows exactly what is missing—for example:
   - no behavioral proof of the graphics;
   - no deterministic multiplayer check;
   - screenshots alone are insufficient.
3. It preserves your source, launch path, team and draft.
4. It offers only actions that can actually work:
   - revise using those findings;
   - grant another bounded attempt;
   - change provider;
   - stop and resume later.
5. Time spent reading or answering prompts does not consume provider-working time.
6. Once accepted, DeadReckon confirms everything and creates exactly one Job.

In short: today it says “something is wrong—try again” while retaining neither useful feedback nor usable time. It should say exactly what is wrong, preserve your progress, and provide a recovery action that is guaranteed to run.

_**User (2026-08-05 20:14:30Z)**_

what is the simplest consolidated way to fix this uniformly

---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-05 20:15:03Z)**_

The simplest consolidated fix is to introduce one `StartAdmissionSession` that owns the entire pre-launch process.

Today, each START phase manages its own errors, timing and partial state. The session should instead own:

- Selected source, launch path, provider and team.
- Current phase.
- Remaining automated-work budget.
- Draft contract and exact validation findings.
- Whether each failure is retryable.
- The actions that are genuinely available.

Every phase would return a typed result such as:

```rust
enum AdmissionFailure {
    RetryableProviderError,
    RevisionRequired { findings: Vec<Finding> },
    BudgetExhausted,
    ConfigurationError,
    SourceConflict,
    SupervisorUnavailable,
}
```

Then one central recovery function decides what to offer:

- `RevisionRequired` → show findings and offer Revise.
- `RetryableProviderError` with time remaining → offer Retry.
- `BudgetExhausted` → offer a new explicitly bounded attempt or Stop.
- Configuration or source failures → show the specific corrective action.
- Never display an action that cannot execute.

The timing rule should also live in that session:

```text
available time = minimum of:
  overall admission remainder
  per-phase limit
  explicit deadline remainder
```

Only automated provider work consumes the work budget. Time spent answering prompts does not. Choosing Retry never silently resets the overall budget.

Generated drafts and findings should remain attached to the session. They should be written into the project only after acceptance. Ideally, the session is checkpointed so restarting `deadreckon start` can resume it.

This does not require rewriting every START component. Keep the existing source resolver, planner, contract author and supervisor checks, but make them all run through the same admission-session wrapper.

The single acceptance test for the architecture is:

```text
fail at any START phase
→ preserve all earlier selections
→ report the exact cause
→ offer only executable recovery actions
→ resume from that phase
→ create zero or exactly one Job
```

That gives you one uniform fix boundary instead of continuing to patch each newly exposed seam.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-05 20:33:00Z)**_

The regression suite now exercises the real distinctions the CLI needs to make:

- deterministic rejection offers Revise, not blind Retry;
- the revision prompt contains the exact missing clauses and weak checks;
- the rejected YAML/Markdown is fed back to the next author without becoming project authority;
- exhausted work offers an explicitly named new bounded attempt;
- an expired absolute deadline offers only Stop;
- operator prompt time leaves provider-work time unchanged;
- course planning cannot steal the contract author’s entire allowance.

The Rust test binary is recompiling after those additions; once it lands I’ll run the real fake-Codex compatibility test and iterate on any failures.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 01:04:56Z)**_

The fault is now pinned down:

- After final confirmation, START creates the durable Job and freezes a workspace-capture policy.
- `/Users/gdc/test-deadreckon` is a non-Git parent directory containing several sibling projects, each with its own nested `.gitignore`.
- `workspace_capture.rs` compiles each nested ignore file with that subdirectory as its matcher root, but then applies every matcher to every sibling path.
- `ignore::Gitignore::matched_path_or_any_parents` correctly panics when, for example, a matcher rooted at `super-mario/` receives a path under `flight-recorder-demo/`.

The fix belongs in the frozen-ignore traversal, not in START or panic handling: retain each matcher’s scope and skip it for paths outside that scope. I’ll first add a sibling-project regression that currently panics, then implement that scoped matching and verify both core capture and full START suites.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 04:19:59Z)**_

Diagnosis is complete, and the implementation itself was correct:

- Claude changed `purpose.sh` correctly.
- The native deterministic gate passed the exact shell acceptance check.
- The failure was produced in [semantic_judge.rs](/private/tmp/deadreckon-release-083.7yefie/source/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/semantic_judge.rs:1125): the structured-output schema allows any string as an evidence citation, even though the prompt and parser allow only six fixed IDs.
- Claude therefore returned an embellished citation such as `source-diff: purpose.sh changed …`.
- The parser rejected that at [semantic_judge.rs](/private/tmp/deadreckon-release-083.7yefie/source/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/semantic_judge.rs:1045), and [turn_loop.rs](/private/tmp/deadreckon-release-083.7yefie/source/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:5314) correctly failed closed to `needs_review`.

The minimal fix is to encode those six IDs as an enum in the output schema and add a regression assertion. I’ll verify it with the semantic-judge tests, both real-provider routes, and the full suite. Your instruction to loop the release through failures covers this scoped remediation, so I’m applying it at the schema layer now.
